newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian state seeks Asian bans in labour dispute.
newsitem.headline: Australian state seeks Asian bans in labour dispute.

text.p: Australian trades union leaders said on Wednesday they might ask colleagues in Asia to impose international trade bans to support industrial action in Western Australia state over new labour relations laws.

After a day of strikes which saw air links to the state cut on Tuesday, late-night talks between state premier Richard Court and Jenny George, president of the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU), failed to resolve the dispute.
"We've indicated that we'll pursue this campaign industrially, politically, with community support, nationally and internationally if necessary," George told a news conference in Perth.
ACTU assistant secretary Tim Pallas said there was strong support within the ACTU for pursuing trade sanctions from Asia.

"I don't want to say at this stage that it is a certainty because no final decision has been made, but we are already preparing lists of companies with major export operations who are seen as being supportive of this legislation," he said.

"It will ultimately be our decision, but I've got to tell you that our sentiments and our feelings at the moment are that it probably will occur...as a formal request to our international colleagues in the next week or two," Pallas told the news conference.
A state union spokesman said later that unions in Japan, South Korea, Vietnam, the Philippines, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India and Malaysia had already expressed support for the campaign.

A representative from the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions, Dan Gallin, who arrived in Perth on Monday, was also at Wednesday's news conference and described the legislation as "a direct attack on unions".
The state government's labour relations bill was expected to be debated in parliament on Thursday after already being passed in the lower of the two houses of parliament.
The bill includes provisions that would limit union access to worksites and employee wage records and demands that unions hold pre-strike secret ballots.
Trade unions have dismissed the legislation as imposing unreasonable restrictions on their operations in breach of internationally-recognised human rights.
Thousands of workers around the state took part in a "day of action" on Tuesday to protest against the legislation. The strikes principally affected construction and manufacturers.
All international and domestic air links to Perth were also interrupted for 24 hours and ports remained closed.
